title: Rental Agreements in India: What You Are Actually Signing
seoTitle: Rental Agreements in India: Clause by Clause
description: What an Indian rental agreement really contains, why it runs 11 months, what registration is worth, and the clauses to fix before you sign it.
excerpt: Two pages, signed in eight minutes, and every line of it load-bearing. Here is what an Indian rental agreement actually says, why it is always 11 months, and what to change before you sign.

author.role: Renters who have read the clause nine too late

faq.q: Why are rental agreements in India always for 11 months?
faq.a: Because of the Registration Act, 1908, which requires a lease from year to year or for any term exceeding one year to be registered. An 11-month agreement sits below that threshold, so owners avoid registration, stamp duty and the public record it creates. It is a cost-avoidance workaround rather than a legal requirement — nothing stops you registering an 11-month agreement if you want the stronger evidence.

faq.q: Is a notarised rental agreement the same as a registered one?
faq.a: No, and the difference matters. A notary attests that these two people signed this document on this date, which is useful and cheap, but the notary does not verify who owns the property and notarisation does not satisfy the Registration Act. Registration means the agreement is presented at the sub-registrar office or a state tenancy portal, duty is paid, and it enters the public record. Registration is far stronger evidence in a dispute.

faq.q: Does the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 apply to my rental agreement?
faq.a: Only if your state has enacted its own tenancy law based on it. The Model Tenancy Act was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021, but tenancy is a state subject and a model law is a template the centre circulates for states to adopt, adapt or ignore. Its recommendations — including a two-month residential deposit cap and a Rent Authority — bind nobody until a state legislates. Check your own state before relying on any of it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a lock-in period and a notice period?
faq.a: A lock-in is the minimum time you are committed to stay; leaving earlier usually means paying rent for the balance or forfeiting part of the deposit. A notice period is how much warning either side must give to end the tenancy. They interact: with a two-month notice inside a six-month lock-in you must give notice by month four to leave at month six. Check that both are mutual, not one-sided.

faq.q: How much stamp duty do I pay on a rental agreement in India?
faq.a: It depends entirely on your state. Stamp duty on tenancy documents is set at state level and the calculation can depend on the rent, the deposit and the length of the term, so any single national figure you read is wrong somewhere. Most states now use e-stamping, and the state stamp or registration department website is the only source worth trusting for the current rate.

faq.q: What clauses should I get changed before signing a rental agreement?
faq.a: Push for a mutual lock-in and mutual notice period, a deposit refund timeline stated in days with any deductions itemised in writing, an explicit exclusion of normal wear and tear, notice before the owner enters, and a repair threshold that applies per repair rather than per year. Ask to strike automatic forfeiture of the whole deposit and any blanket liability for damage that was already there. Get the draft a day early so you have time to ask.

body:
Meera signed her Pune rental agreement standing in a parking lot, on the bonnet of the owner's car, because the printout had arrived late and both of them had somewhere else to be. Two pages, stamp paper stapled to the front. She checked the rent, the deposit and the eleven-month term, signed both copies, and got her keys.

Nine months later she was offered a job in Hyderabad and had to move early. That was when she finally read the rest of the document.

Clause 9: a lock-in period of twelve months.

Twelve months of lock-in inside an eleven-month tenancy. It wasn't a clever trap. It was a template somebody had downloaded, half-edited and printed, and neither of them had read it. The owner was as surprised as she was — and then, being a reasonable person having a bad month, held her to it anyway, because it was there in writing and his flat was now empty in a slow season.

Meera paid two months' rent for a flat she didn't live in.

Here's the thing about rental agreements in India: everybody treats them as a formality, right up until they become the only thing that matters.

## The document is short, and every line of it is doing work

A standard residential rental agreement — called a leave and licence agreement in Maharashtra and a few other places — usually runs two to five pages. It isn't a complicated document. That's exactly why nobody reads it. It looks harmless.

Here's what's normally in one, and what each part is actually for.

**The parties.** Full names, addresses, and usually ID numbers of the owner and the tenant. The name here should match the name on the property documents. If it doesn't — if you're signing with a son, a brother-in-law, a caretaker — you need to know why, and you want a power of attorney or the owner as a co-signatory. This is one of the quiet places where [rental scams](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) begin.

**The premises.** Full address, floor, flat number, area, and often a schedule of what's included: the parking slot number, terrace access, a store room. If your parking slot isn't written down, you don't have a parking slot. You have a habit.

**The term.** Start date and end date. Almost always eleven months. More on that in a moment.

**Rent.** The amount, the date it's due, and how it's paid. Look closely at whether rent is stated as inclusive or exclusive of maintenance. That one word is worth a few thousand rupees a month.

**Security deposit.** The amount, and — if you're lucky — when and how it comes back. Deposits are a whole subject of their own and [worth preparing for properly](/blog/security-deposits-in-india).

**Maintenance and outgoings.** Who pays society maintenance, property tax, electricity, water, gas, internet, and what happens to non-occupancy charges. Frequently vague. Often expensive.

**Use.** Residential use only, usually. How many occupants. Sometimes restrictions on pets, on subletting, or on running any kind of business from the flat.

**Lock-in and notice.** Two different clauses that people confuse constantly. See below.

**Repairs.** Who fixes what, and the rupee threshold that splits the two.

**Termination, renewal and escalation.** What each side can do and on what grounds, whether the agreement renews, and by how much the rent goes up if it does.

**Inspection.** The owner's right to enter, and with how much notice.

**Indemnity, jurisdiction, dispute resolution.** Boilerplate that suddenly matters if you ever need it.

Then two signatures, two witnesses, and often photographs of both parties pasted onto the last page. That's the whole thing. Two to five pages. Read them.

## Why every agreement runs eleven months

Ask ten renters why their agreement is eleven months and you'll get ten guesses. It isn't a convention and it isn't arbitrary.

Under the **Registration Act, 1908**, a lease of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, must be registered. Compulsory. Not a suggestion.

Registration means a trip to the sub-registrar's office, stamp duty and a registration fee, and a public record of the tenancy.

Eleven months sits just under that threshold. So the entire country writes eleven-month agreements and renews them, over and over, for tenancies that in practice run five years.

Two consequences are worth understanding.

First, this is cost avoidance, not a legal requirement. Nothing stops you registering an eleven-month agreement. Some states would rather you did — several now run rent-authority registration portals, and where a state tenancy law is in force, reporting or registering the tenancy may itself be mandatory.

Second, an unregistered agreement is weaker evidence. It isn't worthless. But it was deliberately structured to stay off the official record, and that's not the strong position most people assume they're standing in when a dispute starts.

## Stamp paper, notary, registration — three different things

Most people use these words interchangeably. They aren't the same, and the difference is exactly what your agreement is worth if you ever have to prove something.

**A printout on stamp paper.** The agreement is executed on stamp paper — or e-stamped, which most states now use — and signed by both parties and two witnesses. Stamp duty on a tenancy is a state matter: the rate, and how it's calculated, varies from state to state, and can depend on the rent, the deposit and the term. Don't trust a number you read on the internet, including this article. Check your own state before you pay it. What this gives you is a properly stamped contract between two people, admissible in court. What it doesn't give you is any independent check that the people who signed are who they say they are.

**Notarisation.** A notary public attests the signatures. This is what most agreements in India get, because it's cheap and fast. It adds a third party who has confirmed that these two people signed this document on this date, and it's widely accepted as address proof. But notarisation is *not* registration — a notarised agreement for a term exceeding a year does not satisfy the Registration Act — and a notary does not verify that the person signing actually owns the flat.

**Registration.** The agreement is presented at the sub-registrar's office, or through the state's online tenancy portal where one exists, stamp duty and a registration fee are paid, and it enters the public record. This is the strongest version. The date is fixed, denying it is hard, and in a dispute you're producing an official record instead of a sheet of paper from your drawer.

A blunt rule of thumb: the bigger your deposit and the longer you plan to stay, the more registration is worth. On a short stay with a one-month deposit, notarised stamp paper is what almost everyone does, and it's a defensible call.

## The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a template, not the law where you live

This is the single most misreported thing about renting in India, and you'll find confident, well-designed, high-ranking articles that get it wrong.

In June 2021 the Union Cabinet approved the **Model Tenancy Act, 2021**. It's a genuinely sensible document. It proposes a cap on security deposits — two months' rent for residential premises, six for non-residential. It requires written tenancy agreements and their reporting to a Rent Authority. It sets notice requirements before an owner can enter. It creates a Rent Authority, a Rent Court and a Rent Tribunal so that disputes don't have to crawl through ordinary civil courts.

And it binds nobody.

Land and tenancy are state subjects. A model law is a template the centre circulates for states to adopt, adapt or ignore. Until *your* state enacts its own tenancy legislation, the Model Tenancy Act does not govern your agreement, your deposit or your notice period. Some states have moved. Many have not. Several still run on much older rent control laws that behave quite differently.

So when someone tells you the law now caps deposits at two months, the honest reply is: which state? Check your own state's position before relying on any of it, and be a little suspicious of anyone who describes a nationwide rental law in India without naming one. What [tenant rights](/blog/tenant-rights-in-india) you actually have depends on where you're standing.

## Lock-in, notice, renewal, escalation

Four clauses. People confuse the first two constantly, and Meera's story is what that costs.

**Lock-in period** is the minimum time you're committed to. Leave earlier and you typically owe rent for the balance of the lock-in, or forfeit part of the deposit. Owners want it because re-letting costs them a vacant month and a hunt for a new tenant. Six months is common. Twelve months on an eleven-month agreement is nonsense, and if you see it, it's a template error to get corrected before you sign, not after.

Two things to check. Is the lock-in *mutual*? One that binds you while letting the owner terminate on a month's notice isn't a lock-in, it's a one-way commitment. And how does it interact with the notice period? Because —

**Notice period** is how much warning either side must give to end the tenancy. One or two months is standard. Ask three questions: is it the same both ways, does the clock start from written notice, and can you pay in lieu of serving it?

The trap is the arithmetic. Two-month notice inside a six-month lock-in means you must give notice by month four to leave at six. Miss that date and you're paying for month seven.

**Renewal.** Does the agreement renew automatically, or simply expire? Auto-renewal on the same terms is convenient. Auto-renewal on terms the owner sets later is not. The safest wording says it may be renewed by mutual written consent — and puts the escalation in writing now.

**Rent escalation.** Most agreements carry an annual increase on renewal. A single-digit percentage is the norm in most cities. What matters more than the number is that a number exists at all. An unspecified escalation means an annual negotiation from a position where moving costs you a deposit, a weekend and a fortnight of your evenings.

## Maintenance: who fixes the geyser

This is where money quietly leaks, and it's usually the vaguest section in the document.

The generally accepted split: the owner handles structural and major repairs — seepage, plumbing inside the walls, the roof, structural cracks, replacing appliances that fail from age. The tenant handles minor day-to-day upkeep and anything they broke. Fuses, tap washers, bulbs, cleaning, sometimes pest control.

Most agreements draw that line with a rupee threshold. Repairs under some amount are the tenant's; above it, the owner's.

That pattern is fine and it prevents a lot of small arguments. Three things to check before you agree to a number.

1. **Is the threshold per repair, or per year?** Per repair is normal. Per year is a much worse deal wearing the same sentence.
2. **Does it apply to appliances the owner provided?** If the fifteen-year-old geyser dies of old age, that isn't your maintenance item, and the clause should say so.
3. **What about society maintenance and non-occupancy charges?** Many societies charge owners a non-occupancy fee on a rented flat. Some owners try to pass it on. Negotiable — but only before you sign.

While you're there, settle who pays for pest control, water tankers in the dry months, and servicing anything with a filter. Add them up and you'll find the [true monthly cost of a flat](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) is rarely the rent on the listing.

## Clauses to add, clauses to strike

You have more room to negotiate than you think, especially before money changes hands. Politely, in writing, over email.

**Ask to add:**

- A clear deposit refund timeline in days from handover of keys, with deductions itemised in writing and backed by bills
- An explicit line that normal wear and tear is not deductible
- A signed inventory and condition report, attached as an annexure
- Notice before the owner enters — twenty-four hours is reasonable, and it's the idea the Model Tenancy Act uses
- A mutual lock-in and a mutual notice period, in matching language
- Named responsibility for the things that actually break in Indian flats: geyser, inverter, water motor, tanker supply, pest control
- What happens if the flat becomes uninhabitable — a long water cut, a serious leak, a building repair
- Permission for small reversible changes: curtain rods, wall hooks, a water purifier

**Ask to strike or fix:**

- A lock-in longer than the term. Yes, this really appears.
- Any clause letting the owner enter without notice
- Automatic forfeiture of the entire deposit on early exit
- A repair threshold set so low that everything becomes yours
- An undefined escalation on renewal
- A blanket clause making you liable for damage that was already there
- A requirement to repaint the whole flat at your cost regardless of how long you stayed — negotiate it to something proportionate, or at least know you agreed to it

If the owner won't move on a single line, that's information about the next eleven months.

## Before you sign, photograph these

Ten minutes with your phone. Note that this isn't the flat — that's a separate walkthrough, and there's a [checklist for the viewing itself](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india).

- **The owner's ID**, and the name on it matched against the name in the agreement
- **The property document** — sale deed, allotment letter, or the latest property tax receipt — showing who owns this flat
- **The society NOC**, if the building requires one for tenants
- **Every page of the agreement, signed**, annexures included, before you hand the copies back
- **The stamp paper or e-stamp certificate**, with its number and date visible
- **Both meter readings** — electricity and water — on the day you take possession, with the meter number in frame
- **Receipts for the deposit and first month's rent**, plus the bank transfer confirmation

Then email the lot to yourself. Phones get lost and stolen. Email doesn't.

## The mistakes that cost the most

**Signing without reading, because everyone is standing up.** Ask for the draft a day in advance. An owner who won't send it a day early is telling you something.

**Not checking who owns the flat.** The person collecting rent and the person who owns the property aren't always the same, and when they aren't, your agreement may be worth less than you think.

**Taking only one signed copy, or none.** Both parties sign both copies. You keep one.

**Assuming a verbal promise survives.** The owner said you could keep a dog, repaint the second bedroom, add a flatmate. If it isn't in the document it evaporates on the day it becomes inconvenient.

**Letting the last months' rent be adjusted against the deposit.** It sounds efficient. It quietly destroys your leverage at exactly the wrong moment.

**Ignoring the notice-period arithmetic.** Set the calendar reminder for the date you'd have to give notice. Today, while the number is in front of you.

**Treating renewal as automatic.** Diary the expiry a month early and start the conversation yourself, rather than being handed a new number in week eleven.

## A few things you only learn by renting

**Get the draft by email, not WhatsApp.** You want a searchable document and a version history, not a photograph of a page.

**Read clause numbers out loud when you disagree.** Talking about clause 9 instead of about trust changes the temperature of the conversation. It becomes a document problem, not a character problem.

**A short, plainly written agreement beats a long, impressive one.** Some of the worst are ten pages of borrowed legal language neither party understands, containing three clauses that contradict each other.

**Keep everything in one folder** — agreement, annexures, receipts, meter photos, the email thread. Physical or cloud, doesn't matter. What matters is that eighteen months later it takes thirty seconds, not an evening.

**Renewal is the best moment to renegotiate.** The owner doesn't want a vacant month either. If a clause hurt you this year, that's when to change it.

**Ask your questions before the agreement is drafted, not after.** Half of what ends up in a bad clause was never discussed at all — there's a [list of questions worth asking](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) long before anyone opens a template.

## Where StayOnMap fits, honestly

We don't draft your agreement, we don't hold your money, and we can't make an owner accept a clause. A rental platform claiming otherwise would be overselling.

What we can do is narrow the information gap that makes the paperwork so lopsided in the first place.

Every listing on StayOnMap states rent, deposit and maintenance as required fields, so those three numbers are on screen before you visit — rather than appearing on stamp paper you're reading in a parking lot. There's no brokerage. And you contact the owner directly, which means the person you ask about the lock-in is the person who decides it, not a middleman relaying an answer.

The homepage is a map, because what's genuinely near a home is a fact you should be able to check for yourself instead of taking on trust. If you want the longer version of why we built it that way, [we've written about that too](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home).

That's the honest scope. Better information earlier, fewer people in between, and the numbers stated up front.

## What to remember

An Indian rental agreement is two to five pages, and every clause in it is load-bearing. Eleven months is a workaround around the Registration Act, 1908, not a rule. Notarisation and registration are different things, and only one of them puts your tenancy on the public record. Stamp duty varies by state — check yours, don't take a figure from an article. And the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a template the centre circulated, not a law that governs you unless your state has enacted its own.

The document takes fifteen minutes to read properly. Ask for it a day early. Read the lock-in and the notice period twice, and do the arithmetic between them.

Meera reads agreements now. All of them, on a laptop, the evening before. Her current one in Hyderabad has a six-month mutual lock-in, a two-month mutual notice period, and a repair threshold she argued down over three emails.

It took her forty minutes.

It cost her two months' rent to learn.
